Hedge Of Protection
hej uv pro-TEK-shun
noun phrase
A prayer-meeting idiom — 'we ask a hedge of protection around them' — drawn directly from Satan's complaint about Job: 'Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side?' (Job 1:10). The image is a thorny boundary God sets about His people to keep harm out; the phrase is biblical in source, but has become a rote formula through sheer repetition.

See also: Hedge of Protection

⚖️ Biblical Verdict

🟡
Neutral
Sound biblical imagery from Job 1:10, merely worn rote by overuse — a gentle call to mean it and pray it in submission.

📖 Biblical Definition

The image is genuinely scriptural and rich. In Job, the accuser concedes that God has 'made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side' (Job 1:10) — a divine protection so real that Satan could not touch Job until God lifted it. The same protecting care runs through Scripture: 'The angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them' (Ps. 34:7); 'As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people' (Ps. 125:2); 'thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy' (Ps. 61:3). To pray a hedge of protection, then, is to ask God to be about His people as He was about Job — sound doctrine and a fitting prayer. The only caution is the Job context itself: the hedge is God's to raise and to lower for His own wise purposes, so the prayer must be offered in submission, trusting His protection and His permitted afflictions alike.

📜 Origin & Era

A biblical image (Job 1:10) of God's protecting boundary about His people; sound imagery worn merely rote by overuse — a gentle call to mean it, and to pray it in submission to the God who raises and lowers the hedge.

HEDGE OF PROTECTION, noun phrase. God's protecting boundary set about His people to keep harm out.

Source: Job 1:10, Satan's concession that God had 'made an hedge about' Job and all he had.

Sound imagery, echoed in Ps. 34:7, Ps. 125:2, Ps. 61:3 — the LORD round about them that fear Him.

Caution is only rote-ness: the phrase is often repeated mechanically; and Job's context shows the hedge is God's to raise and lower in His wisdom.

📖 Key Scripture

Job 1:10 — "Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side? thou hast blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land."

Psalm 34:7 — "The angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them."

Psalm 125:2 — "As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever."

Psalm 91:1 — "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty."

Psalm 5:12 — "For thou, LORD, wilt bless the righteous; with favour wilt thou compass him as with a shield."

Zechariah 2:5 — "For I, saith the LORD, will be unto her a wall of fire round about, and will be the glory in the midst of her."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Drawn from Job 1:10, the image is sound and the prayer fitting; the only fault is rote-ness — a phrase repeated mechanically. A gentle call to mean it, and to pray it in submission to the God who both raises and lowers the hedge.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, and indeed faces no real corruption at all — the phrase is biblical in source and sound in sense. The image comes straight from Scripture: Satan, in Job 1:10, is forced to admit that God had 'made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side.' That hedge was a true and effective protection; the accuser could not lay a finger on Job until God Himself drew it back. To ask the same protecting boundary for the saints — that the Lord would be 'round about his people' as the mountains are round about Jerusalem (Ps. 125:2) — is faithful prayer in faithful words. The only thing to examine is not the doctrine but the heart of the one praying: whether the phrase has gone limp through endless repetition into a thoughtless filler reached for at every prayer meeting, the lips moving while the mind sleeps.

There is a second, gentle caution drawn from the very passage the phrase quotes. In Job, the hedge is God's hedge — His to set and His to lift — and He lowered it, for holy reasons Job could not see, that His servant might be tried and in the end more blessed (Job 1:12; 42:12). So the prayer for a hedge must never harden into a demand that God shield His people from all affliction, as though protection were owed and suffering a sign of failed faith. The same God who hedges may, in wisdom, permit the storm; 'shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?' (Job 2:10). The prayer is offered, like all prayer, in submission to His will (Matt. 26:39), trusting both the hedge He raises and the trials He permits.

The recovery, then, is simply to mean it. Let 'a hedge of protection' be prayed with the weight Job's account gives it — a real plea to a real God who really compasses the righteous 'with favour... as with a shield' (Ps. 5:12) and is 'a wall of fire round about' His city (Zech. 2:5). Pray it thoughtfully, not by rote; pray it in submission, not as a demand; and let the familiar words carry the living faith they were meant to carry. A worn coin is still gold; the cure for a rote prayer is not to discard it but to pray it from the heart.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

A biblical image (Job 1:10) of God's protecting boundary about His people; sound and fitting, faulted only by rote repetition. Mean it, and pray it in submission to the God who both raises and lowers the hedge.

English: a prayer-meeting idiom drawn directly from Job 1:10, Satan's concession of the 'hedge about' Job.

Biblical echoes: Ps. 34:7, Ps. 125:2, Zech. 2:5 — the LORD encamped round about, a wall of fire, mountains about Jerusalem.

The caution from Job: the hedge is God's to raise and lower (Job 1:12) — pray it in submission, not as a demand against all affliction.

"God hedged Job and then, for holy reasons, lowered the hedge — pray for protection in submission, not as a demand."
